cards.heading: The four agent loop patterns
cards.question: What are the four recurring shapes an agentic loop takes?
cards.answer: Retry, plan-execute-verify, explore-narrow, and human-in-the-loop — each fitted to a different kind of task and each with its own characteristic failure.

cards.heading: Retry loop: fit and failure
cards.question: What task fits a retry loop, and how does it characteristically fail?
cards.answer: Short atomic tasks with a clean pass-or-fail line; it fails by repeating the same broken approach indefinitely without an explicit variation or escalation rule.

cards.heading: Plan-execute-verify: fit and failure
cards.question: What task fits plan-execute-verify, and how does it characteristically fail?
cards.answer: Multi-step work where order matters and an early mistake compounds; it fails by over-committing to a plan that turns out wrong partway through, unless it can revise the plan.

cards.heading: Explore-narrow: fit and failure
cards.question: What task fits explore-narrow, and how does it characteristically fail?
cards.answer: Genuinely unfamiliar territory; it fails on cost, since running several approaches in parallel consumes context and tokens, so early aggressive pruning matters most here.

cards.heading: Human-in-the-loop: fit and failure
cards.question: What task fits human-in-the-loop, and how does it characteristically fail?
cards.answer: Anything whose wrong assumption is expensive to unwind; it fails by interrupting so often that the person saves no time by having an agent involved.

cards.heading: Why human-in-the-loop is first-class
cards.question: Why does this taxonomy treat human-in-the-loop as a first-class pattern rather than a fallback?
cards.answer: It makes the interruption points a deliberate design decision chosen for stakes, instead of the thing that happens when the automation simply gives up.
